findings_matched.gt_title: Malicious executable p.exe in attacker staging directory
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same process: p.exe with PID 8260, running from C:\Windows\Temp\Perfmon\p.exe, launched by cmd.exe (PPID 5948), created 2018-08-30. The agent finding adds detail about the user account (spsql/Domain Admin) and loaded DLLs suggesting C2 capability, while the GT focuses on the RWX memory region and prefetch evidence. These are complementary observations about the same primary subject — the malicious p.exe process in the attacker staging directory.

findings_matched.gt_title: Attack conducted under spsql account with Domain Admin privileges
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: the attacker's PowerShell process running under the spsql account with Domain Admin privileges. The GT focuses on PID 5848 while the agent finding references PID 8712, which may be a different PowerShell instance, but both identify the spsql account (RID-1193, Domain Admin) as the execution context for the attacker's PowerShell. The agent finding provides additional mechanism detail (WMI-based spawning via WmiPrvSE) while the GT focuses on the privilege/integrity level. The shared subject — spsql account with Domain Admin context running attacker PowerShell — is the primary observation in both findings, making this a match despite the PID discrepancy and differing levels of mechanistic detail.

Both findings describe the same network observation: multiple TCP connections from 172.16.6.11 to 172.16.4.10 on port 8080 in ESTABLISHED and CLOSE_WAIT states, with no clear PID association preserved. The agent finding is more specific (breaking down connection counts and attributing indirectly to p.exe), while the GT notes the orphaned PID situation similarly. The core subject — C2 communications to the same remote endpoint on the same port with the same connection states — is identical.

findings_matched.gt_title: PowerShell C2 shell with stealth flags
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same process: powershell.exe PID 5848, a 32-bit SysWOW64 instance spawned by PID 8712 with identical command-line flags (-Version 5.1 -s -NoLogo -NoProfile). Both identify it as a C2/remoting shell used to drop/execute p.exe via cmd.exe. The agent finding provides additional detail about the -s flag semantics and AMSI evasion rationale, while the GT emphasizes duration and rundll32 children, but the primary subject and core observation are identical.

findings_matched.gt_title: Six short-lived rundll32.exe instances from PowerShell C2 shell
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the exact same observation: powershell.exe PID 5848 spawning six rundll32.exe child processes (PIDs 6768, 5452, 5588, 4108, 2216, 8148) over the same time window (2018-08-30 18:31 to 2018-08-31 00:56 UTC). The mechanism (PowerShell spawning rundll32 children), the parent PID, the child PIDs, and the timestamps all match precisely. The agent finding adds detail about blank command lines and frames it as reflective DLL loading during a staging phase, while the GT notes short lifetimes and mixed 32/64-bit architecture — these are complementary details about the same underlying observation, not different mechanisms.

findings_matched.gt_title: Outbound lateral movement via SMB and RDP
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe outbound lateral movement from the same host to the same two internal targets (172.16.7.15 on port 445/SMB and 172.16.4.5 on port 3389/RDP), identifying this host as a pivot point. The agent finding is more specific — it adds a second ESTABLISHED SMB connection to 172.16.4.5 and notes seven CLOSED RDP connections rather than one — but the core observation (SMB and RDP lateral movement to those two internal hosts) is the same. The minor discrepancy in connection counts and states does not change the fundamental subject or mechanism being described.

Both findings describe the same negative observation: no registry-based persistence was installed by the attacker. Both specifically reference the spsql user hive Run keys being empty and svcscan finding no malicious services. The agent finding is more specific (enumerating exact registry paths, naming specific benign services found) but the core observation is identical to the ground truth.

Both findings describe the same artifact: procdump.exe located at the identical file path within the Dashlane application directory. Both reference it as a Sysinternals credential dumping tool and flag it for investigation in the context of a compromise. The agent finding is more specific (noting no running process, speculating on staging), while the GT notes the possibility it could be a legitimate Dashlane component. These are complementary framings of the same observation, not different mechanisms or subjects.

findings_matched.gt_title: PowerShell (PID 8712) malfind hits are .NET CLR heap segments, not injection
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same observation: malfind flagging three RWX regions in powershell.exe (PID 8712) that are actually benign .NET CLR managed heap segments, identified by the 0xFFEEFFEE/0xEEFFEEFF signature. Same process, same PID, same tool, same mechanism (CLR heap allocation), same conclusion (benign). The agent finding is slightly less detailed (omits the null-byte prefix and self-referential pointer metadata) but clearly describes the same observation.
